title: From a photo to a resin figurine

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Picture a photo of your dog, and a few steps later a little glossy vinyl-style figure of that dog sitting on your desk. That's the pipeline Antoine wrote up, and it runs on four simple steps.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Four steps? Okay, walk me through them. Where does a photo even begin to turn into something you can hold?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Step one is a clear reference photo, side or front view. Step two turns it into a chibi vinyl toy image: a smooth plastic character with a big head, one subject, white background, a pose that can stand on a base. ChatGPT or Midjourney can do that, or you can do it inside ComfyUI with a model called OmniGen2.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So the photo becomes a cartoon toy first. Why not go straight to 3D?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Think of it like a sculptor's sketch. A clean, simple 2D toy image gives the image-to-3D model a clear silhouette to follow. Antoine's page makes the point that a clear toy picture matters more than which 3D tool you pick.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Step three is the mesh. Hunyuan3D version 2 reads the toy image and builds a 3D model. Antoine packaged the whole thing as one ComfyUI graph you can load. Stage A runs OmniGen2 to make the chibi picture, and stage B runs Hunyuan3D to export two 3D files, at thresholds of point seven and point six, so you can compare them.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Nice, two versions to choose from. And if you don't have a beefy computer?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: The page lists hosted options too, like RodinHD, Hi3DGen, Meshy and Tripo3D. You upload the toy picture, preview the result, and tune face count, symmetry and remeshing before you export.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Right. Step four is resin printing, which suits small parts. You tilt overhangs toward the build plate, add light supports on things like hair and capes, and check for floating islands in the slicer or in a free tool called UVtools. The page shows the finished figurines.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: There's even a handy guide. A gift figurine from a pet photo? Use a chatbot toy image, then a hosted mesh tool. A repeatable local batch? Use the ComfyUI file. Teaching a class? Use the slide deck.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That's the takeaway. Start with a clean toy image, let the model build the mesh, print in resin, and you've gone from photo to object. The full write-up has the diagram, the slide deck, the ComfyUI file and the finished prints.
